591.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and chant the Lord's Name. O very fortunate ones, earn this wealth.”
591.explanation: Guru Arjan calls for udam, active effort, and names the Lord's Name as the wealth that such effort earns.
591.tie_back: The Kural says only those with inner energy truly possess anything; Guru Arjan likewise ties real wealth to effort, though the wealth he means is the Name, not property.
591.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 48, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
591._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both make effort (udam, ookkam) the ground of true possession, but the Kural speaks of worldly capacity and Gurbani of spiritual wealth.

592.quote_or_event: “Your wealth shall not go with you; why do you cling to it, you fool?”
592.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan reminds the listener that riches are left behind and are no fit object of attachment.
592.tie_back: The Kural sets the lasting possession of an energetic mind against wealth that slips away; Guru Arjan shares the verdict on wealth, though what he sets against it is the Name rather than drive.
592.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
592._accuracy_note: Partial: the transience of wealth is common ground, but Gurbani's lasting good is the Name, not the Kural's energy of mind.

593.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust”
593.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person in whose heart God dwells as one who is not shaken by suffering and values gold no more than dust.
593.tie_back: The Kural says those who firmly hold energy do not grieve over lost wealth; Guru Tegh Bahadur's steady person likewise does not lament loss, though his steadiness comes from detachment rather than confidence in winning wealth back.
593.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
593._accuracy_note: Partial: refusing to grieve over loss matches, but Gurbani grounds it in equanimity, the Kural in the energy that will regain prosperity.

594.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace.”
594.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan promises that sustained effort brings life and that its practice brings peace.
594.tie_back: The Kural says prosperity itself asks the way to the home of the person of unwavering energy; Guru Arjan likewise makes good fortune follow from effort.
594.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
594._accuracy_note: Reasonable: reward following effort is shared, but in context Guru Arjan's effort is devotion to the Name and the reward is spiritual peace, not material prosperity.

595.quote_or_event: “O my mind, you are the embodiment of the Divine Light - recognize your own origin.”
595.explanation: Guru Amar Das tells the mind that its true nature is divine light and calls it to know that source.
595.tie_back: The Kural says a person rises only as high as the mind, as a water-flower's stalk rises with the water; Guru Amar Das likewise places a person's true height in the mind, though in its divine source rather than its drive.
595.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441, Raag Aasaa, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
595._accuracy_note: Next-best: both make the mind the measure of a person's stature, but the Kural means energy and aspiration, Gurbani the divine light within, and the water-flower image is not shared.

596.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
596.explanation: Guru Nanak asks total commitment, even readiness to give one's life, from anyone who would walk the path of love for God.
596.tie_back: The Kural asks that every thought be lofty and says such an aim keeps its worth even if fate defeats it; Guru Nanak's call to set out with head in hand, whatever the cost, is the closest Sikh counterpart.
596.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
596._accuracy_note: Partial: both prize an uncompromising aim regardless of outcome, but Guru Nanak speaks of devotion and self-surrender, not worldly aspiration.

597.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
597.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns the Gurus included in the Guru Granth Sahib, defines the true hero (soora) as one who fights for what is right and holds his ground even as he is cut down.
597.tie_back: The Kural's war elephant, pierced deep with arrows, still stands firm; Kabir's hero, cut piece by piece yet never leaving the field, gives the same picture of steadfastness in ruin.
597.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
597._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both use the battlefield to show firmness that does not give way even when wounded, though Kabir adds that the cause must be righteous.

598.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
598.explanation: Guru Nanak joins honest labour (kirat karni) to sharing (vand chhakna): one who earns by his own effort can give from his own hand.
598.tie_back: The Kural says those without energy of spirit will never know the joy of being generous givers; Guru Nanak likewise makes one's own labour the basis of true giving.
598.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
598._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit: both tie generosity to one's own exertion, though Guru Nanak means everyday sharing, not a patron's pride in munificence, which Sikhism would see as ego.

599.quote_or_event: “The Lord is like sugar, scattered in the sand; the elephant cannot pick it up. Says Kabeer, the Guru has given me this sublime understanding: become an ant, and feed on it.”
599.explanation: Kabir says the great elephant, an image of pride, cannot gather the sugar of the Lord from the sand, while a tiny ant can.
599.tie_back: The Kural's huge, sharp-tusked elephant takes fright before a tiger, showing that bulk does not decide a contest; Kabir also shows the great elephant beaten by something small, though what wins for him is humility, not energy.
599.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir (238), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
599._accuracy_note: Next-best: the shared lesson is that size does not prevail, but Kabir's ant stands for humility while the Kural's tiger stands for energy and courage.

600.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
600.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says of those who live without the Name that they have human birth but not human worth.
600.tie_back: The Kural says those without inner energy differ from trees only in having human shape; Guru Arjan likewise denies full humanity to those who have the form without the substance.
600.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
600._accuracy_note: Reasonable: the structure is the same, human in form but not in worth, though Gurbani means lack of devotion and the Kural lack of energy.
